Planted mangroves in Hainan, China, cut mean wind speed behind the stand by 59.4% during typhoons, a result cited in a review [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_mcivor12_1]. In northern Viet Nam, mangrove planting is credited with keeping a sea dyke undamaged in a 2005 typhoon and cutting the share of shrimp-farm value destroyed from 90 to 25 per cent [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ifrc11_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ifrc11_2]. In Gujarat, India, 74 of 227 households surveyed reported reduced cyclone and storm damage after mangrove planting [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_becklange16_1], project staff in coastal Bangladesh state that mangrove afforestation has reduced loss of life and property in cyclones [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_1], and a World Bank evaluation in the Mekong Delta finds farming protected from storms, wind and salt where reforestation succeeded [ev_frmg_vnppar_8].
caveats: Every unit here concerns planting, but none is a controlled measurement: the Viet Nam results are before-and-after reports by evaluators of the implementing programme [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ifrc11_1], the Gujarat result is what households recalled, with no comparison villages, reported in grey literature [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_becklange16_1], the Bangladesh statement comes from the project's own staff [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_1], and the Hainan figure is cited second-hand [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_mcivor12_1]. None of the evidence is from a severe or extreme cyclone. The same Mekong evaluation found the coastline moving inland where seedlings were planted too small and not monitored, so the benefit depends on the planting succeeding [ev_frmg_vnppar_8]. Part of the protection falls beyond the farm, on dykes, ponds and villages.

mitigation_mechanism: Cyclones can cause moderate damage to mangrove stands. After Category 5 Typhoon Odette in the Philippines, 85.71% of trees in planted stands were damaged against 77.14% in natural stands [ev_climate_shock_baring24_1], and most of the Rhizophora stylosa deaths, 14 trees, were in planted plots [ev_climate_shock_baring24_2]. Red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle) was significantly less resistant to hurricane damage than black mangrove (Avicennia germinans) in the French Caribbean [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_3], and a review reports higher death rates for Rhizophora trees in strong winds [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_gijsman21_2]. In the French Caribbean, Hurricane Hugo stripped 19% to 71% of the trunk area from the worst-hit stands [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_1], and recovery took about as long as the usual gap between hurricanes, so stands may never fully recover [ev_climate_shock_imbert18_2]. In Florida, 62% of mangroves suffered canopy damage from Hurricane Irma, worst in tall forests [ev_climate_shock_lagomasino21_1], and in Australia Cyclone Debbie damaged 18.1% of mangrove trees in the affected area [ev_climate_shock_rowl26mg_1]. Newly planted stands in Vietnam and Bangladesh were also lost or badly damaged by storms before they established [ev_frmg_vnppar_6, ev_frmg_vnppar_7, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_ahammad13_4]. In Australia, Category 5 Cyclone Yasi caused severe windthrow on 16% of 13,795 ha of mangroves, worst in Rhizophora stands as winds passed 280 km/hr [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_1], and many damaged areas showed no or very limited recovery, with canopy cover falling from above 90% to below 20% [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_2]. In the Florida Keys, tree mortality after Hurricane Irma rose to 36.6% after 9 months, and to 19.8% at a less hard-hit site [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_1, ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_2]. A review puts full recovery of a hurricane-damaged forest at 20–30 years, given enough time between hurricanes [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_2]. For planted stands, hurricanes on St Croix were partly to blame for losses the year after a restoration planting [ev_climate_shock_krauss23_1], and after Typhoon Haiyan in the Philippines mangroves younger than 8 years fully recovered within 2 years while those older than 32 years had 95% mortality [ev_climate_shock_asbridge18_3]. mitigation_mechanism: Sediment burial can harm mangroves, but how much depends on how much sediment arrives and how fast. Heavy or sudden burial caused dieback: in Sarawak, Malaysia, the decline of Sonneratia alba in the inner part of a natural stand was attributed to burial of its breathing roots, and no new roots had formed on the dead trees [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]; on the Mekong coast of Vietnam, forest density fell moving inland as root burial deepened, citing the authors' own earlier measurements [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1]; and large, sudden sedimentation events can bury many trees in a short time and cause large-scale dieback, as also reported, second-hand, along a river in Indonesia loaded with volcanic sediment [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2]. Reviews citing earlier work add that rapid sedimentation can cause delayed death of trees by smothering their aerial roots [ev_establishment_survival_gijsman21_1, ev_climate_shock_ellis04_3], and that the effect depends on the sediment's texture and on how much arrives and how fast [ev_climate_shock_woodroffe16_1]. In Florida after Hurricane Irma, trees under a thicker layer of storm-deposited mud were more likely to die in the following months, though the mud did not affect how many died at first [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_3]. Mild burial and slow build-up did little harm. In a New Zealand estuary with sedimentation as high as 23 mm a year, mangroves at the muddiest sites were taller, had more breathing roots and new seedlings and were less stressed [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1], though the site with the most sediment showed more deaths of breathing roots and seedlings, which the authors call a potential negative effect [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_2]. In a seedling experiment in China, every species survived a modest burial treatment except the small pioneer Sonneratia apetala, of which 2 of 12 seedlings died [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_2].
caveats: The damage is rated low because only the mild cases give a size: the New Zealand sedimentation rate and the seedling experiment, where harm was small [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1, ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1]. The findings of heavy or sudden burial killing trees state no size [ev_climate_shock_muro99_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2], so the low rating should not be read as saying planted mangroves are safe from heavy burial. The field evidence comes from natural or partly natural stands, not from stands stated to be planted; the Vietnam and Indonesia cases are second-hand, and the Sarawak result is a single transect [ev_climate_shock_fagh17_1, ev_climate_shock_fagh17_2, ev_climate_shock_muro99_1]. The seedling experiment was short and tested only a modest burial dose [ev_climate_shock_vhes22_1], and the New Zealand stand is a single-species system in a high-income, temperate setting [ev_climate_shock_ellis04_1]. The Florida result is from a single hurricane in a high-income setting and gives no size either [ev_climate_shock_radabaugh19_3]. Part of the effect is off-site rather than on the adopting farm.
